You can wear this, OK?
also: Now get dressed, quick.
The morning Dad forces Harry onto the boat - Miles takes off his own necklace.

Brotherhood & Loyalty symbolism Parrett's symbolism in Miles's plain line 'You can wear this, OK?' turns the shark tooth into an object of protection passed between brothers, so a single object comes to embody the loyalty and self-sacrifice binding the brothers together. Family Secrets & Inconsistency challenge assumptions The tragic irony of 'You can wear this, OK?' is that the same tooth later damns Harry in Dad's eyes, inviting the responder to challenge assumptions about what an act of love can cost. Memory, Grief & Hope individual and collective Read as a motif , the tooth Miles hands over with 'You can wear this, OK?' protects Harry individually while standing for the family's inherited history of loss, linking one boy's experience to a collective human experience of grief.
Miles rips the tooth off like a Velcro strap and clips it onto Harry's neck like a coach buckling a rookie's helmet before sending him onto the field.
First-choice for 2021 (how individuals respond to challenges) and 2019 (loss) - a gift of protection that ironically causes a greater loss.

every cell in his body stopped
Harry alone on the beach at Cloudy Bay, holding an old abalone shell.

Memory, Grief & Hope stylistic features shape meaning Parrett's short, almost clinical sentence 'every cell in his body stopped' renders a child's collision with mortality in bodily rather than abstract terms, a distinctive stylistic feature shaping how the responder feels the moment. The Ocean as Threat individual and universal Though the moment is private, the physical imagery of 'every cell in his body stopped' captures a dawning awareness of death that every reader recognises, a universal human experience the module asks students to connect to their wider world . Memory, Grief & Hope structure shapes meaning As foreshadowing , 'every cell in his body stopped' plants Harry's own death in the novel's opening pages, showing how structure can shape meaning long before the event arrives.
Harry holds an ancient abalone shell and his whole body freeze-frames like a paused video, faint ghost outlines of long-dead people standing around him on the sand.
First-choice for 2019 (reconsidering your understanding of loss) - the moment before any loss has actually happened.

because of him . Because of you.
Dad, holding the tooth, tells Miles why their mother was leaving.

Family Secrets & Inconsistency grammatical features shape meaning Parrett's anaphora in 'because of him. Because of you' fragments Dad's accusation into two short blows, enacting his blame-driven state of mind, a grammatical feature the rubric says can shape meaning . Violence & Power inconsistencies in behaviour The shift from third to second person in 'because of him. Because of you' exposes the motive behind years of Dad's cruelty to Harry, direct evidence of the rubric's inconsistencies in human behaviour and motivations . Memory, Grief & Hope challenge assumptions The bitter irony of 'because of him. Because of you' is that a grieving father blames a child for his mother's leaving, inviting the responder to challenge assumptions about who deserves blame.
Dad jabs a finger first at a photo of Uncle Nick, then swivels and double-taps Harry's chest, like a courtroom lawyer pointing at two suspects in a row.
First-choice for 2024 (motivations and actions) and 2022 (emotions arising from human experience) - the family-secret reveal in five words.

How could that man know his name ?
Harry bolts from George Fuller's shack - a stranger calls him by name.

Family Secrets & Inconsistency anomalies and inconsistencies Parrett's interrogative sentence 'How could that man know his name?' is left deliberately unanswered, planting an inconsistency the reader cannot yet resolve, a direct instance of the rubric's anomalies, paradoxes and inconsistencies in human behaviour . Family Secrets & Inconsistency ignite new ideas The narrative gap after 'How could that man know his name?' keeps the responder questioning the Curren family's past long after the scene ends, exactly the module's demand that a text ignite new ideas . Memory, Grief & Hope challenge assumptions As foreshadowing , the unanswered question 'How could that man know his name?' plants George's unexplained tie to the boys' dead mother, deepened later by the white lilies in his shack that reappear on her crash tree, an anomaly the novel never resolves, inviting the responder to challenge assumptions about the man the town calls a monster.
A shack door creaks open and a booming game-show-host voice bellows 'HARRY CURREN, COME ON DOWN!' - except Harry never told a single soul he was there.
First-choice for 2023 ('ignite ideas about collective human experiences') and Pymble 2024's prompt on anomalies that make you ' see the world differently ' - almost nobody else will quote this line.

Dad even brushed Harry’s hair back then
Miles remembers what Dad used to be like, in the same memory as Mum and the lucky curls.

Family Secrets & Inconsistency inconsistencies in behaviour Parrett's characterisation through a single habit in 'Dad even brushed Harry's hair back then' shows a tenderness the same hands later betray when Dad shakes Harry 'like a rag doll', a direct instance of the rubric's inconsistencies in human behaviour and motivations . Family Secrets & Inconsistency stylistic features shape meaning The small adverb 'even' in 'Dad even brushed Harry's hair back then' marks the gesture as unexpected, so one word carries the whole characterisation , the kind of stylistic and grammatical features the rubric says can shape meaning . Memory, Grief & Hope human experiences of loss Placed inside Miles's memory rather than the present, 'Dad even brushed Harry's hair back then' frames Dad's kindness as something already lost, widening the novel's exploration of loss beyond Mum's death alone.
Picture gentle past-Dad in a shampoo advert, carefully brushing Harry's curls with a tiny doll's hairbrush - the exact opposite of the Dad who shakes Harry later.
First-choice for 2024 (qualities, motivations and actions) and Shore 2024's trial line that 'moments of inconsistency are crucial to crafting powerful stories.'

He was just a kid. A baby. He was nothing.
Miles, moments before the 'stuck' line, thinking about how outmatched he is.

Responsibility & Entrapment stylistic features shape meaning Parrett's collapsing tricolon of short sentences 'He was just a kid. A baby. He was nothing' strips Miles down clause by clause until nothing remains, using sentence length itself as a stylistic feature to enact his erasure. Brotherhood & Loyalty anomalies and paradoxes The paradox of 'He was just a kid. A baby. He was nothing' is that the boy who feels like nothing is the one holding his whole family together, direct evidence of the module's anomalies, paradoxes and inconsistencies in human behaviour and motivations .
Mid-sentence, Miles shrinks into a nappy-wearing baby standing on a giant reef, then a rubber stamp slams down the word 'NOTHING' over him like a rejected passport.
First-choice for 2019 (reconsidering your understanding of loss - the loss of self-worth, not just a person) and 2024 (qualities, motivations, actions).

Miles was careful to split the food equally
Beans and mash for dinner, just the two of them - Miles serves Harry's plate first.

Brotherhood & Loyalty human qualities Parrett's understated domestic detail of Miles being 'careful to split the food equally' shows a boy quietly parenting his brother without ever being asked to, a human quality of self-sacrifice the Common Module asks responders to recognise. Responsibility & Entrapment human experiences Parrett's indirect characterisation of Miles choosing to 'split the food equally' turns one small act into evidence of poverty and premature responsibility, an individual quality that also carries a shared human experience of hardship. Brotherhood & Loyalty anomalies and paradoxes The paradox buried in 'split the food equally' is that the child who should be cared for has become the carer, an inconsistency in ordinary family life that lets the responder see the world differently .
Picture Miles as a lab-coated scientist with a jeweller's scale, weighing two single baked beans against each other so neither brother gets one extra gram.

First-choice for 2024 (the ' complex relationship between human qualities, motivations and actions ') and the Kambala 2024 trial prompt on Harry's experience with Dad and one other person - Miles's quiet parenting is that other person.
Priority 1 · memorise first
Responsibility & Entrapment Brotherhood & Loyalty
Stuck working for Dad, stuck being responsible for Harry
Miles on the cliff, after Joe warns him he'll get stuck.

Responsibility & Entrapment grammatical features shape meaning Parrett's anaphora in 'Stuck working for Dad, stuck being responsible for Harry' hammers entrapment home as an inescapable condition rather than one bad day, a grammatical feature mirroring Miles's grinding, repetitive life. Responsibility & Entrapment reflect personally The blunt repetition of 'stuck' in 'Stuck working for Dad, stuck being responsible for Harry' names an experience of inherited responsibility many readers recognise, letting them reflect personally as the rubric intends. Brotherhood & Loyalty individual and collective Read collectively, the same repeated adjective in 'stuck being responsible for Harry' speaks for every child forced to grow up early because the adults around them failed to, extending one boy's entrapment into a collective human experience.
Miles is superglued to the boat's steering wheel, a label-maker stuck to his forehead endlessly printing 'STUCK STUCK STUCK STUCK.'
First-choice for 2021 (how individuals respond to challenges) and 2025 (endurance of the human spirit under a burden not of his choosing).

He let himself cry.
Miles with Joe, being told about all the places they'll go.

Brotherhood & Loyalty human qualities Parrett's blunt short sentence 'He let himself cry' marks the single moment Miles's restraint finally breaks, the syntax itself performing the release of emotion the rubric calls a human quality. Memory, Grief & Hope endurance of the human spirit Parrett's diction in 'He let himself cry' suggests crying required permission, exposing the cost of everything Miles has endured, direct evidence for 2025's focus on ' the endurance of the human spirit .'
A tough action-hero Miles finally lets one single cartoon teardrop go *plink* onto Joe's shoulder, like a dam springing its first tiny leak after years holding firm.
First-choice for 2025 (endurance of the human spirit); doubles as the emotional payoff for 2021 (responding to challenges).
Priority 2 · next
Family Secrets & Inconsistency Violence & Power
I never wanted you.
Dad's voice through the walls as the boys flee into the scrub.

Family Secrets & Inconsistency inconsistencies in behaviour Parrett compresses the novel's central paradox into four blunt words, 'I never wanted you' - the parent who should protect instead rejects, precisely the inconsistencies in human behaviour and motivations the module asks students to examine. Family Secrets & Inconsistency structure shapes meaning The unspecified second-person pronoun in 'I never wanted you' is aimed at no one, since Parrett has Dad 'Yelling at them, at everyone. Yelling at no one', so only on rereading, knowing Dad suspects Harry is his brother's son, does that 'you' settle onto Harry, a delayed cruelty showing how structure can shape meaning . Violence & Power structure shapes meaning Through the auditory imagery of 'brown walls,' Dad's 'I never wanted you' reaches the boys as disembodied sound rather than direct address, so the responder, like Miles and Harry, experiences rejection as something beyond their control.
A giant loudspeaker bolted to the house wall blasts these four words so loud the night sky visibly cracks open like a comic-book sound effect.
The single most common Past the Shallows quote - kept only because nothing shorter says as much; use for 2022 (emotions arising) but do not rely on it alone.
Priority 2 · next
The Ocean as Threat Violence & Power
the water was angry
Dawn on Dad's boat off Bruny - Miles reads the surface for danger.

The Ocean as Threat language shapes representations Parrett's personification of 'the water was angry' makes the sea a living, hostile presence the boys must learn to read rather than a backdrop, the kind of language choice the rubric says is used to shape these representations . Violence & Power symbolism Read symbolically , 'the water was angry' doubles the sea's rage with the anger simmering inside the Curren house, so one image works literally and figuratively at once.
The ocean grows a scrunched-up cartoon face with steam hissing from wave-shaped nostrils, shaking an angry fist-wave at Miles's little boat.
Good opening evidence for 2022 (emotions arising through the features of prose fiction ) and for setting up any answer about nature and family as parallel threats.

These are like Mum’s cups
Harry drinking tea at George's place after Dad's beating - he notices the cups.

Family Secrets & Inconsistency stylistic features shape meaning Parrett's use of an ordinary object as a motif in Harry's remark 'These are like Mum's cups' quietly links George Fuller to the boys' dead mother, showing how a small stylistic feature can carry an unspoken family secret. Family Secrets & Inconsistency view of the world Parrett's use of subtext after 'These are like Mum's cups' invites the responder to draw the connection themselves, enriching a ' view of the world ' in the way the 2023 question describes. Memory, Grief & Hope individual human experiences As a symbol , the cup behind 'These are like Mum's cups' gives Harry a physical link to a mother he is losing more of every day, grief experienced through ordinary objects rather than dramatic scenes.
Harry lifts a teacup at George's table and it's printed with Mum's ghostly face - and the whole room goes dead silent.
A genuinely niche choice - first pick for 2023 (ignite ideas that enrich our view of the world ) and any 'particular lives' question (2025), since almost no study guide covers this detail.

shook him like a rag doll
Dad grabs Harry after he uses the radio in protected waters.

Violence & Power human experiences Parrett's simile 'shook him like a rag doll' strips Harry of humanity in the instant of violence, reducing a child to an object, a stark human experience of powerlessness the module asks responders to examine. Family Secrets & Inconsistency inconsistencies in behaviour Set against the memory of Dad brushing Harry's hair, the juxtaposition in 'shook him like a rag doll' places past tenderness directly beside present violence, embodying the rubric's inconsistencies in human behaviour .
Dad grabs Harry and shakes him exactly like a floppy ragdoll pegged to a washing line - arms and legs flapping like wet spaghetti.
First-choice for 2021 (challenges individuals face) and Fort St 2024's 'complex emotional responses' - pairs directly with the hairbrushing quote as a before/after argument.

This ocean could hold you down
Miles swimming out to Harry in the huge swell after the boat capsizes.

The Ocean as Threat human experiences Parrett's personification in 'This ocean could hold you down' gives nature agency and indifference, so human will counts for nothing against it, an unsettling human experience of powerlessness. Responsibility & Entrapment endurance of the human spirit The flat declarative 'This ocean could hold you down' states the danger flatly, yet Miles keeps swimming through the breaking waves toward Harry regardless, the clearest evidence for 2025's question on ' the endurance of the human spirit .'
A giant blue hand rises out of the sea and presses down on Miles's head like a schoolyard bully doing a wedgie - except the bully is the entire Tasman Sea.
First-choice for 2025 (endurance of the human spirit) and strong for 2021 (individuals responding to extreme challenges).

p. 9 · Prologue
black and cold and roaring
The very first line of the novel, describing the dark water past the shallows (also echoed on the last page).

The Ocean as Threat language shapes representations Parrett's polysyndeton in 'black and cold and roaring' slows the line and stacks three threats on top of each other, introducing the ocean as the novel's real presence before a character has appeared. Memory, Grief & Hope structure shapes meaning As a structural motif , 'black and cold and roaring' resurfaces almost unchanged on the final page, making the sea's danger and its promise the same water, differently understood by a reader who has now lived the novel.
A lion made of black seawater roars once at the very start of the book and once at the very end - like the MGM lion, but soaking wet and terrifying.
Best paired with 'To somewhere warm. To somewhere new.' as a two-quote 'bookend' argument for 2020 (how the text tells stories) or 2023 (ignite ideas).
Priority 3 · if time
Memory, Grief & Hope Family Secrets & Inconsistency
They were all baby things .
Miles finds a box in Aunty Jean's cupboard while she cuts his hair.

Memory, Grief & Hope human qualities and emotions Parrett's symbolism in the discovery that 'They were all baby things' suggests a child Aunty Jean once wanted but never had, showing the module's interest in human qualities and emotions extends to minor characters. Family Secrets & Inconsistency see the world differently The understatement of 'They were all baby things' leaves Miles, and the reader, to work out that the hard, controlling aunt has a private grief boxed away at the back of her own linen cupboard, an anomaly in human behaviour that invites the responder to see the world differently .
Aunty Jean's cupboard box pops open like a jack-in-the-box, but instead of a clown, tiny baby socks and blankets spring out and float sadly around the room.
Good for 2023 (collective human experience - grief isn't only the boys') and Kambala 2024's prompt on Harry/Miles's experience with 'one other person.'
Priority 3 · if time
Memory, Grief & Hope The Ocean as Threat Brotherhood & Loyalty
To somewhere warm. To somewhere new.
The final two lines of the novel, right after George returns the tooth.

Memory, Grief & Hope structure shapes meaning Parrett's cyclical structure returns the prologue's 'invisible paths' as 'To somewhere warm. To somewhere new' so the reader leaves the novel by the same water they entered it by, now carrying hope, structure shaping meaning across the whole text. Memory, Grief & Hope ignite new ideas The anaphora of 'To somewhere warm. To somewhere new' turns the ocean from a threat into a promise, letting the ending ignite new ideas about what survival can lead to. Brotherhood & Loyalty individual and collective The repeated indefinite adverb in 'To somewhere warm. To somewhere new' never names the destination, leaving Miles's and Joe's future open rather than fixed, extending Miles's survival into a shared, collective human experience of moving on after loss.
A glowing golden GPS arrow rises out of the final wave and points, dead certain, straight at a tiny sunny cartoon island in the distance.
First-choice for 2025 (endurance of the human spirit) and 2023 (a text that can 'ignite ideas... that enrich our view of the world ') - most guides quote only the opening, not this deliberate echo.

What am I meant to do? What am I meant to do?
Aunty Jean, in the same scene, talking about selling Granddad's house.

Memory, Grief & Hope human experiences Parrett's repetition of a rhetorical question in 'What am I meant to do? What am I meant to do?' voices Aunty Jean's desperation directly and without narration, showing that even background adults carry unresolved human experiences. Responsibility & Entrapment anomalies and paradoxes The inconsistency beneath 'What am I meant to do?' is that her grief for her father curdles into a grievance about deserving something, exactly the kind of anomalies, paradoxes and inconsistencies in human behaviour and motivations the rubric describes.
Aunty Jean stands in the driveway holding a giant red question-mark balloon, and it visibly inflates bigger each time she repeats the line.
Useful for 2022 (emotions arising from human experience); pair with the baby-things quote from the same scene to argue two different emotions from one character.
